utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Case IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. As we've had some very bad weather this morning and we are short of time, I'd like to say hello to everybody, and, Mr. Registrar, would you give me the IC numbers that we need.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. [In English] The parties have provided lists of documents to be tendered through Witness CR. The list provided by the OTP will be given Exhibit number IC 196. The list provided by 1D will be provided Exhibit number IC 197. The list provided by 2D will be given Exhibit number IC 198. The list provided by 3D will be given Exhibit number IC 199. The list provided by 4D will be given Exhibit number IC 200. And the list provided by 5D will be given Exhibit number IC 201. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just a very quick point in relation to the sniper expert. Your Honour made some comments on Tuesday this week - that's at page 1183 of the transcript for the reference - and Mr. Scott was invited to provide some further information. Your Honour, our understanding is that we now have until this coming Monday to respond on the Defence side, and our suggestion and request is that our response should follow after, but very shortly after Mr. Scott has dealt with those queries. What would be most helpful as a practical matter - we know that everybody has lots of things to do - is if Mr. Scott were able to provide that information preferably today but certainly before the week -- ah, they're here. It looks as if they're on their way. Your Honour, that will solve the problem then. We should then be able to discuss the matter with our clients and deal with it on Monday, if that is the full answer to those questions. So that's very happy news.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. What I do have available today is a chart, if you will, that can be helpful in explaining the expert report and the annex to the indictment at page -- paragraph 114, and I'm prepared to pass these out at this point in time and perhaps I can give a very brief explanation as to what exactly happened I would -- if perhaps the -- or the court usher could assist with that, that would be helpful. We can deal with this issue very quickly right now. Just to briefly explain what had happened in the initial indictment there were 14, if you will, representative or sample sniping incidents. The expert was provided with certain information to do his report based upon those 14 scheduled incidents. The Prosecution in order to preserve the privacy of the victims and witnesses gave information to the expert with the use of pseudonyms that were assigned for that limited purpose for the expert which is why the names don't appear in the expert report. Following the production of that expert report and during the process of amending the indictment, two of those representative sample incidents of sniping were removed from the indictment based upon, in part, the conclusions reached by the expert. As a result, the annex, the confidential annex description of paragraph 114 lists 12 scheduled sniping incidents. The expert report, however, continues to refer to all 14 because, as I said, that was done prior to the amended indictment and the amended confidential annex thereto. The table that we have just produced has the actual numbers in the left-hand column as referred to in the expert report. You will note that there is no incident 5 and there is no incident 12 because those are the two of the original 14 that the Prosecution does not list in the paragraph 114 in the annex. The far right-hand column are the names of the specific victims or witnesses who will testify about each of those scheduled incidents, and I believe if I recall correctly seven of them are the actual named victims and five of them are witnesses, and I believe what we've done is we've put this document in bold the name the victim and when they're the witness similarly that name in the right-hand column appears in bold. If there's a name that's not in bold then that is not the victim who will testify but another witness. And again, due to the nature of this material on this document, we have marked it confidential and we would ask that it be treated as such by all the parties to whom it's been provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. So it is thanks to this table and column that we have the relationship between the incidents and the victims. There are 12 individuals, and you put the -- down the victims that can testify. That's one preoccupation settled. Now, I have another concern and it is this: If among the victims I'd like to know whether there were any local investigations, ballistic expertise, medical expertise, things like that, because that could be useful to us. And the third element that is lacking here from my point of view, and I think that my colleagues share my sentiments, is that with respect to the sniping, these sniping incidents, what is important for the Judges is to know the positions of the snipers, of course, and the area, the zone from which the shooting came, to know under whose control that area was. Now, in the expert report, as far as I was able to see looking through it, there's nothing like that. So my concerns are that we're going to spend a week and then be able to conclude that there was a sniping from point A that hit victim X in -- who was in area B without getting us any further than that. You see, Mr. Mundis, the problem I'm having here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely, and thank you, Mr. President, for again allowing us to briefly respond. With respect to the first query that you've just raised, to the best of the Prosecution's knowledge no investigations were conducted by the local authorities concerning these incidents. What we can say and what we are prepared to produce in terms of the evidence when these victims come are what we have used in prior sniping cases, and the best example of course being the Galic case with respect to the siege of Sarajevo. There are what we have produced and disclosed known as 360 degree photographic evidence that can be used with the victims and witnesses to point out particularly where they were at the time they were shot and where they believe or where they have reason to believe that the sniper was located at that point in time. That information is also reflected, as Your Honour has noted, in the expert report with respect to suspected or known locations where snipers were active. With respect to the second point, and we do believe that this 360 degree evidence is quite helpful to the Trial Chamber. As Your Honour may or may not be aware, it was used extensively in the Galic case and was some evidence that the Prosecution led with respect to sniping -- the sniping campaign in the city of Sarajevo. With respect particularly to the second issue, again based on the practice that was used in the Galic case and which the Galic Trial Chamber relied upon in its judgement as confirmed by the Appeals Chamber was precisely the type of evidence that indicates that where a known sniper location or where the evidence points to a sniper being on one side of the confrontation line is certainly sufficient evidence to demonstrate that that sniper was under in effect the control of the authorities or the military units in that area, so what may or may not be possible to establish is the actual identity of the actual perpetrator, the actual sniper. It may or may not be possible in all instances to identify which unit or units was at the location, but what we were able to do, and I can speak from experience having had responsibility for the sniping campaign for Sarajevo in the Galic case was that to show that the victim was on one sign of the line and the shots came from the other side of the line was about as far as we could take in the Galic case many of those sniping incidents, and that was sufficient both for the Trial Chamber and the Appeals Chamber in the Galic case. So with those caveats, Your Honours, and combined with the other evidence that is led as to where the confrontation lines were at the relevant time periods, we believe we can establish the -- the side, in effect, which was conducting the sniping with respect to these victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, with distinct reservations on the Defence side in relation to the submissions which are inherent in what's been said this morning, we appreciate the clarity of the explanation of the Prosecution's position. That is helpful. And it's also particularly helpful not just as Your Honour had indicated to have the victims identified but equally or in this case -- well, at least as important as the identification of the prospective witnesses in relation to these incidents where they're different people. Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't want to prolong this discussion unduly, but the question that you yourself raised is I think a key question for the expertise, that is to say whether the expert had medical material, autopsies in case of death or detailed descriptions in case of being wounded. And of course witness statements and so on. That is basic forensics. If we don't know the position at which the victim was when they were killed, what position the entrance and exit wound, then there is no possibility even theoretical for us to be able to conclude anything about the sniping. So if there are no medical documents, then it really will be a waste of time, to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We would just in brief response to that, we would anticipate that some of the witnesses who will be testifying either as victims or witnesses will have medical reports with them and again the witnesses will provide the information that my learned colleague, Mr. Kovacic, is referring to. The last point if I could just -- I neglected to do this earlier. I would ask that the sheet that I just submitted be provided with an IC number so that in the future if we need to refer to it everyone is referring to the document by an IC number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really don't want to prolong this. However, it is -- my basic concern, and that's why we're having this discussion today, is whether the presentation of that evidence is that we're going to waste one week in this courtroom without the Trial Chamber receiving the relevant information and material, and that is why spending time on that is valuable. But bearing in mind my learned friend's answer, if it doesn't matter whether the -- it doesn't matter whether the expert witness is going to bring in this material but whether the expert had access to that, because he can determine on the basis of the victim's position where the shot came from. Now, if he doesn't know that, if he doesn't know what side the witness was turned on, what the entrance and exit wound was or just entrance wound and the bullet lodged in the body, we're speaking about basic forensic facts here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you -- the Defence has until the 15th of January to file a written response, so please put it all down in writing by that will deadline, by the 15th of January. We have taken note of what you have said, and we shall be making a ruling very shortly. May we have an IC number for this document under seal of course.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit number IC 202, Your Honours, under seal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just ask for confirmation, it is correct the witness will be giving evidence in English. The report's in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, he will.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's have the witness shown in now, please. I would like us to proceed as quickly as possible. Mr. Mundis said he needs 10 to 15 minutes. We have another witness to get through today after the cross-examination. So please bear that in mind. Mr. Mundis, once the witness has come in, I would like to start off by asking him a question, one that the Trial Chamber considers necessary. So I'm going to ask him that question first which will give us a general picture of the situation and complete that picture. So I need to ask him that question, and then I'll give you the floor afterwards. I'd like to take advantage of this opportunity to say that the witness for -- something about the witness for Monday. The Prosecution will have three hours, and the Defence will have three hours. So the witness will be here on Monday and probably Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having said that I'd like to say good morning to the witness. Good morning, sir. Put your headset on, please. Sir, the Chamber has a question to ask you which seems to us to be important. What you have said so far needs to be explained. When you were at Heliodrom, did you know during the several days that you were there that your colleagues or people who were detained in Heliodrom were taken to do any labour outside, forced labour perhaps? Anyway, labour and work outside that could have exposed them to the front line as a human shield. So did you have any knowledge or do you have any knowledge about anything like that having taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the rooms that I was incarcerated in there was no official taking out of detainees to the front line as a human shield or any other form of torture. I know about two or three cases, however, from that particular room when people were - how shall I put it? - they were too nervous to answer questions they were being asked, and so they were taken out to interrogation, and they were beaten there. And I saw with my very own eyes people in solitary confinement cells in the cellar, at least two people, two cases of this, and one of them survived, I believe. But of my neighbours, the people living on the floor above, and we were friends with these neighbours of ours, I had a statement from them about what happened to them on the way to Heliodrom, and in my diary I have noted that down, noted that statement down where it says that they were taken through Mostar to the front line as human shields on the same day that I was already at Heliodrom. Now, the following day they were taken to the lake at Rudnik. It's an artificial lake at Rudnik. I don't know what they did there. I can't remember. I'd have to take a look in my diary. But they were threatened and told they would be killed. They weren't actually killed, and then they were returned to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. Do you have the names of those people or the person who was taken to Rudnik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move into private session, and you can tell me their names in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you. I have not even noticed that we were in private session.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you please be able to agree were me if I say that the SDS at that moment declared it very clearly that it was against the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia and that in case this should happen, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina would establish their own territorial community?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could hear that in public, in the statements issued by the leaders of that party. And one could also hear that they were against the referendum for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then agree with me that the HDZ which represented the Croatian community in Bosnia-Herzegovina clearly and unambiguously stated that it is in favour of the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Together with the SDA they were in favour of the secession.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were for the secession. Please tell me whether the SDA from day one had a clearly defined position with regard to that issue or did it take them some time to finally take a position on the possible secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a far too difficult question for me. I really didn't know how the HDZ and the SDA communicated, so I can't give you a precise answer. I only know that there was some sort of agreement between the two of them that they would jointly defend Bosnia-Herzegovina and that together they would insist on explaining to the voters why they should vote for the independence in the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ante Markovic's parties did not take part in the multi-party elections in Slovenia and Croatia because the foundation of that political party started once those elections had already been over in those two former republics of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with the time line, so I can't answer that question, but it is easily possible that you are right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned that at other electoral rallies, the ones you mentioned were the one in Mostar, in the vicinity of Mostar near Planinica, people were told that should ethnically based parties win, it would happen that in the town of Mostar on one hill there would be Ustasha guns and on the other hill there would be Chetnik guns. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your party equalised the SDS with the Chetniks and the HDZ was equalised with Ustasha. Wasn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. By and large that was the case. The parties were labelled in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your party, was it opposition to the coalition of the ruling parties at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was opposition, and I was surprised to see that Alija Izetbegovic, for example, who acted at the moment when his party was being established as if he was really in favour of democracy, he would not enter a coalition in any non-ethnically based parties. If they had done that, they would have had a majority in the parliament and nobody could later on say that the war was an ethnically based war. This was my opinion at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you then be able to agree with me that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic wanted to enter into a coalition with other ethnically based parties because he wanted to reorganise Bosnia-Herzegovina according to the criteria of ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a lot of statements to that effect, but I can't be his spokesperson. I can't tell you what he wanted. I am inclined to believe that was the case and that is exactly what he wanted, but I cannot testify to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sure you followed the media. In your view, did the political analysts conclude that Alija Izetbegovic had wanted to enter coalition with ethnically based parts in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even in my view he wanted to do that, otherwise the coalition would never have been made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that he wanted to do so because he wanted Bosnia to be organised based on the ethnic criteria.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be the case but not necessarily. There could have been equal ethnic rights across the board. I really don't know what the intention was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, let's remind ourselves of the positions of the SDS, SDA, the HDZ about the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to Yugoslavia, and let's go one step further. Could you then agree with me that among these three political parties there was a difference with regard to the issue of the internal organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that you're trying to drag me into things that are disputable and that require longer explanations. I can only speculate, but I do not have a firm position with this regard and especially not at this moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just asking you whether among them there was a difference with regard to the internal organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. We don't have to go into any detail?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he beginning it was quite obvious that the SDS wanted to separate the part of the territory that they believed was theirs and merge it with Serbia, and the same case was with the HDZ and Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDS stated this after it was decided that there would be a referendum which would decide on the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The SDS declared its wish to establish a sovereign territory within Bosnia-Herzegovina, with the possibility of secession under certain conditions in case Bosnia and Herzegovina seceded from Yugoslavia. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes I could hear it on TV from their leaders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croatian people and the HDZ were they in favour of the survival of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as an independent state? As an independent state and its secession from Yugoslavia? Is that why the Croats took part in the referendum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask me about referendum, there is a lot to say about this referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view, can we repeat the -- the answer, because the interpretation of your answer has been wrongly recorded. My question to you was this: The Croats, when they participated in the referendum, did they allow Bosnia and Herzegovina to become an independent state?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, your new question was worded differently and I can clearly say yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In essence, the question was the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to break for 20 minutes and we're going to resume at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the Defence, two small points. We have been asked to authorise the number of pages for the response concern -- response concerning the witness according to Article 92 bis, and it is dealing with Gornji Vakuf, and the request has been accepted by the Trial Chamber. And another thing is we are going to finish with this witness in an hour and a half. After that, we're going to have a break, and we want to call the next witness after that. Therefore, I'm asking the Defence to speed up. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, we would like to -- I would like to discuss the part of your testimony that deals with the statements on leaving the apartment on your will, and since there is a danger that this part of the questioning might identify you, I would kindly ask the Chamber to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are moving into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. My name is Suzana Tomanovic an attorney from Bosnia-Herzegovina and the co-counsel for Jadranko Prlic. I'm glad to meet you. I'd like to show you a few documents, the first three documents in your set, and I'll start off with that. You told us yesterday that when the HVO took over control in Mostar that it took over control of state enterprises as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that the Muslims' access was limited or prohibited. Would you take a look at the first document. 1D 00447 is the number. And we have here a decision on the appointment of a provisional manager for the DP Enstalater company of Mostar, and the man's name is Hasan Huskovic, the person being appointed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And he's a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Bosniak, quite certainly. Whether he's a Muslim or not I can't say. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, Mr. Jadranko Topic signed this, the president of the HVO municipality of Mostar. Now look at the next document, 1D 00458. And that is another decision on the appointment of a provisional director for the DP Montproject Mostar company.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the interpretation to finish. Now, the person appointed is Miralem Hadziomerovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: He's also a Bosniak, a Muslim; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And once again this is signed by the president of the HVO for Mostar municipality, Mr. Jadran Topic. And now the third document, please, and the number is 1D 00467. Once again a decision on the appointment after provisional director for the DP Stanogradnja company of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The person appointed is Hakija Ljubovic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: He's also a Bosniak and a Muslim, is he not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I've just shown you three documents, three decisions which the Prlic Defence team has out of a total of 11, according to which Bosniak Muslims were appointed directors of companies after May 1992. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've never seen these documents before, but in the first government that was constituted as an HVO government there were Bosniak Muslims among the members. So that confirms it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. And I'd like to show you another document, and for that one perhaps out of an abundance of caution we can move into private session.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: But may I be allowed to finish giving my comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you'll be able to give your comments when the Bench asks you a question or the Prosecution. For me your answer sufficed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in public session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I know that you have a lot of information, but let's focus on what I'm asking you. A moment ago you mentioned, as you said, ingots. You mentioned the ingots which are the raw materials used by the aluminium combine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that for a time that was under the control of the Serbs or it was on Serb-controlled territory, the aluminium factory. And then after that you said when the Serbs left who was in control? In whose hands was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you and I agree that out of these economic organisations, these companies that were the most important ones in Mostar before the war, it was the aluminium factory and the tobacco factory in Mostar, Soko. I'm not asking you about Soko. That's quite true.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soko was a large combine, then there was Djuro Salaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: But what about the two that I mentioned, that they were two the most prominent companies, the tobacco factory and the aluminium factory? Now, let's be very specific and clear. In answer to Mr. Praljak's question you said that nonetheless many of these companies -- yes, I can see that you said that these are two of the most important companies. Your answer was "yes," and it hasn't been recorded in the transcript. So you agree there, your answer is yes, that the tobacco and aluminium factory were two of the largest companies.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tobacco factory wasn't the most important. It was the agrokombinat was very important. The factory farm.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say it was the most important. I said that it was a significant factory. Now, a tobacco factory in peacetime doesn't have the same importance that it has in wartime. I'm just asking you quite simply: Are they two of the -- one of the most prominent or two of the most prominent companies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I want to distinguish between this. The tobacco factory, if I can rank them, in Mostar, it was somewhere in the middle. It wasn't one of the most prominent ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you've put that right, and I agree.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I put that right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the aluminium factory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the aluminium factory was among the first three, the top three factories.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now we can go back to where we left off. Some of those economic resources, or most of them, were in Serb hands at the beginning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And that is what you said in answer to Mr. Praljak's question, that probably they appropriated some of those resources?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they took them away to the cotton industry of Djuro Salaj, the equipment from the Transmisija factory, but I know that from the thermal equipment factory that a lot was taken to Split. Who got that equipment, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the third side, the BH army that we haven't mentioned yet. Can we take a look at document 2D 00305.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel kindly be asked to slow down and make pauses. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: It is the first document in your binder. Yes, I'll do my best to slow down. Thank you. It's the first document and Their Honours have it. Do we see here it is a document of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina of the 4th Corps in actual fact?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to have this document placed on the ELMO. I don't know why we're not getting it on e-court, but here's a hard copy. Two documents. And let's move on. And it says here -- the subject is "Request for the sale of aluminum." 2D 00305. You can look at the document in B/C/S. And it says: "In the brigade warehouse," so that is not challenged, that on the 21st of December, 1992, in the brigade depot or warehouse there were 160 pieces of ingot, of aluminium ingots, with a purity of 99 per cent and total of 116.000 kilogrammes. And small ingots, there were 16.200 kilogrammes of the small ingots; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: So this is a request or demand from Mr. Hujdur asking permission for the sale of these goods because they are goods that are highly sought after on the market and specific goods. So from this, sir, does it emerge that this aluminium factory was in the hands of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the document that's what it would appear.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The date is December 1992. I'll repeat what I said. It would appear to be the case on the basis of that letter.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: And this is a product of the aluminium factory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Otherwise, they couldn't be there, quoted there.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness now place on the ELMO the following document, 2D 00306. I think that will speed matters up. And you can see that the date is the 17th of April, 1993, an order from Mr. Arif Pasalic issuing an order, and it says in the preamble "In order to protect the production capacities and ensure enough cigarettes for the fighters."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you just a point of clarification before it leaves the screen on line 21, page 54. In comparison to what the document says it's a bit -- I'm a bit -- perhaps it's just me, I'm a bit confused, perhaps, but there's reference to it 116.000 kilogrammes and I'm not sure that meshes with what's contained in the document and there's a further reference to weight on line 21, 22 of page 54.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the previous document back on the ELMO. I would kindly ask the usher to return the original of that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Now we can it can we look at it we can see 116.000 kilogrammes. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I can see in the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the B/C/S version there is actually 116.000 kilogrammes, whereas in the English translation there is 116, the comma, and then 000, hence the difference. If the comma was interpreted in the English way, then the weight would be different. It seems that that weight is 116.000 kilogrammes. Mr. Murphy, maybe you know more about the aluminium?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: Not about the aluminium, Your Honour, but that -- just simply about the different ways of writing numbers which I found my cost since coming to live in the Netherlands. There is a difference in practice in England and the United States. Generally when representing 116.000, one would use a comma between the 116 and the three 0's, whereas in the continental practice it's usual to use a period. So in fact the two numbers would be the same allowing for that difference in linguistic practice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, it seems that in the States the comma equals a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I completely agree, and I understand exactly what Mr. Murphy is saying. My only point was there seemed to be a discrepancy between the B/C/S document, the English translation, and perhaps if that could have been clarified. I don't want to spend any more time on it. I think it's pretty clear at this point. I just wanted to call out that the translation doesn't necessarily match the document, and we needed to get that clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]. If Mr. Mundis agrees that in the original version it says without any doubt that the weight in question is 116.000 kilogrammes, then the difference in translation should be in favour of the original document. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we can proceed. Would can proceed. We have the next document that I asked for which is 2D 00306. This is an order bearing the date 17 April 1993 issued by Mr. Arif Pasalic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: He puts under the controlled production and distribution of the factory of tobacco in Sarajevo. I apologise; Mostar. So a commander -- the commander of the 4th Corps puts the production of a civilian product under his control and distribution. But let's move on a bit further. He says out of existing work-force to conduct a selection of most essential workers who are needed for uninterrupted production. And he goes on to say production and distribution to be organised under the authority of the 41st Motorised Brigade which will execute a nomination of management and other workers and regularly conduct a controlled -- control business activities. Were you aware of the fact that the 4th Corps placed under its control the distribution and sales of the products manufactured by the tobacco factory, i.e., the cigarettes at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I entitled to a remark with regards a previous document either now or later.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, neither now nor later. We don't have the time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is technical mistake in that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, but I would like an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tobacco factory is in the eastern part of Mostar which was under the control of the BiH army from the very beginning to the end, more or less, and it is easy to manage that this document refers to the military control of the civilian production. Have I been clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Then you will agree with me that the military control of the civilian production was exercised by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina like you said that some workers on the right banks were controlled by the HVO and that Muslims could not even enter in those companies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The witness says -- I apologise. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am now being confused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak is not in agreement with Mrs. Nozica. What seems to be the matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to hear the comment by Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's too little time, to put it simply. Aluminium is such a complicated manufacture that the -- this production was discontinued with help of French experts who had installed the -- the -- the facilities, and if this had been done with the help of the experts, this would have been a problem. Miro Brajkovic engaged French experts to extinguish the production and it could no longer produce until the end of the war. It just stood idle. My next question: While the Serbs were there did -- and after they left, did he inspect the number of ingots that remained in the factory after they left. If you're not familiar with that information then we cannot speak about the quantities that could have been sold by the HVO after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have now heard a technical explanation. The factory of aluminium, the production there was extinguished and it did not function, and the ingots that should have been produced before existed at the time. What do you think about that? What is your view of that, of that explanation provided by General Praljak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The factory did not manufacture and the problem of its closing down did exist and was handled in the way described by Mr. Praljak. The ingots were not taken away and the document says that they were not taken away. At least not all of them. Maybe some of them were taken away to a certain extent, that could be transported at the time. However, as far as the quantity is concerned, if the 116 pieces are divided by 116.000 kilogrammes it arises that one ingot weighed a tonne, which could not have been the case. 1 tonne could be the weight of the entire pallet that contain the ingot. So either one figure or the other is correct it is 116 piece or 116.000 kilogrammes. As far as the figures are concerned I cannot account for the fact that under the control of the BiH army in their depots there were ingots of aluminium. I really don't know how that happened, how they could come by them because they controlled the eastern side and the western part was only controlled in the central part.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: The intervention by Mr. Praljak was about the document that we already spoke about. The document issued by the tobacco factory of Mostar. However, since you have returned to that document, the mistake that was made either in the number of pieces or the number of the weight was made by the person who drafted the document and how they ended up with the 4th Corps. We don't know, but the fact is that they were stored in the depots of the 4th Corps.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's now move to another brief question. You've been shown document number P 00255, and that is the overview of the number of inhabitants in the local commune around the 25th of May, 1992. When you did that, will you allow for the possibility that by the end of October that number was increased and was about 25.000?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down and allow for the interpreters to finish the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer. Will you allow for the possibility that by October that number increased to 17.000?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the document that was issued by the civilian protection it says that around 30.000 people were present.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I am trying to reduce my questions although I would like to go into detail but I don't have the time. You made an overview on the 25th of May, 1992; is that correct? Let's take things one at a time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: In that overview does it say that the number of refugees and displaced persons at the time in Mostar was about 9.000? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can even say that their number was 10.000.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: But to be more precise, your figure was 8.950. My question to you is this: Is it possible the Prosecution is pointing to the fact that we should go into private session but none of my questions is going to reveal the identity of the witness. So I don't think that is necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Out of an abundance of caution we're going to go into private session. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, before I will put questions to you, I'm going to read out a summary of your statement. The witness was a resident of West Mostar. In February/March 1993, the witness experienced discrimination in receiving humanitarian aid. Her two children were also discriminated against at school. On 9 May, 1993, HVO soldiers came to the witness's apartment and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down when reading the summary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: She was beaten by an HVO soldier. Her husband was arrested and the witness and her children were expelled from their apartment. The witness and her children were taken by bus to Heliodrom. HVO soldiers were guarding the bus which was filled with other women and children. The witness describes the condition of detention in Heliodrom. The witness and her children were released on 16 May, 1993, after signing a document stating that they had been detained at Heliodrom for their own protection. That night, HVO soldiers came to their apartment and expelled them again. They moved into a neighbour's house. Her husband was released from Heliodrom on 26 May 1993. A relative from Croatia came and took her children to Croatia and the witness and her husband went back to their apartment, which had been partially burnt and looted. On 29 May 1993 the witness and her husband fled to East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, this was a summary of your statement and I'm now going to ask you a few questions about the statement that you had given to the Prosecutor. You provided a written statement to the investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY on the 8th of October, 1998. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And at that time you provided this written statement, did you answer the questions to the investigator truthfully?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you answer the questions freely, that is without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: At the conclusion of that interview, was your statement read back to you in the Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And did you then sign that statement in the English language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I now would like you to have a look at the English version of your ICTY statement, and there's a bundle in front of you, and I've marked the page that I would like you to look at with a yellow -- a yellow piece of paper. You see that yellow piece of paper in the bundle? If you -- Maybe the usher can assist the witness. Witness, I've guided you to the last page of the English version of your ICTY statement, and I'm asking you is this -- the signature on the bottom of that page, is that your signature?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yesterday, you met with an investigator and myself, and you were given an opportunity to review your statement in the Bosnian language and to make any corrections, if necessary; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, upon -- Witness, upon reviewing your statement in the Bosnian language, is it correct that you made a correction to a name mentioned in the sixth paragraph on page 9 of the English translation and that this correction concerned the name Marko Vlaho and that you corrected that name to Dragan Vlaho?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I learnt later on that his real name is Drago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you. Should you have to provide a full testimony to this Court today, would its content be the same as the content of the written statement except for the correction that you made regarding Mr. Vlaho?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Witness, I'm now going to show you a couple of exhibits, and I would ask you to comment on these exhibits, and I would like to start with a map. And for that I would like to go into private session, Your Honour, if that's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your statement you also mention -- in the initial part of your statement you say that you could foresee all that based on some signals, and you also say the Croatian language was imposed. This is on page 1 in both B/C/S and Croatian versions. Let me ask you this: The official language in the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia up to the break-up of Yugoslavia, up to late 1990 when the break-up started, could you tell the Trial Chamber what was the name of that language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Was there any other variant of that language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was also a Croato-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So there were two variations that were either Croato-Serbian or Serbo-Croatian. In Bosnia-Herzegovina what language was the official language of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In schools?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: At work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same. It was either Serbian or Croatian or Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So both variants were equally used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And what script was used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Latinic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In both cases?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it depended on the region in Yugoslavia. Some it was the Cyrillic script that predominated and other places that Latinic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm asking you about Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Latinic script.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And in 1991, 1992, there -- the aggression by the JNA started under the control of the Serbian politics and so on and so forth. Did we -- do you think that we had to continue using Serbo-Croatian and use the name of the language that corresponded with the name of the entity that shelled us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You personally, did you believe that Serbo-Croatian is your language when the aggression started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continued speaking the language that I spoke since the day I was born in. That's the language that I am still using today.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you took the liberty to speak the language that you spoke that you know how to speak, irrespective of its name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Would you then agree that people started speaking whatever they thought was right for them to speak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was their right, but they did not have the right to force my child to use that language.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In other words, this is the problem that only applied to schools in your view?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It applied everywhere. When I see some of my acquaintances now, I know how they spoke previously. Now they use terms and words they had never used before. So I find it surprising that they easily forgot what they knew when -- from the day they were born.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: At this moment the Trial Chamber is not interested in any other time but 1992 and 1993. What the situation today is they are -- don't care but let's go back to schools. Do you know whether during the school year 1992, 1993 the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., the authorised ministry, were they able to provide for the school curriculum and syllabuses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No they weren't in a position to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What about books?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Could school books be obtained from Croatia? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Do you know where the school books eventually came from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your children went to school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did but they didn't have school books. They didn't have pens or pencils or notebooks or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic -- Ms. Alaburic, do you have any questions for this witness? Maybe we should leave the next five minutes to Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to check my notes and I have to say that I do have a few more questions for this witness but since my colleague only has five minutes this is where I'm going to interrupt my cross-examination. Thank you. Your Honour, just for the record, please, maybe, I challenge most of the witness's statements in the part of the statement before she was taken to Heliodrom. I challenge that part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness good afternoon I only have four minutes to start with could you explain to us your brief statement when you said that you can't say anything about what happened in 1992 in Mostar because at the time you were in Split; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Split is in Croatia isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How come you resided in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had friends there and I went there with my children I went to Split.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you go for a holiday or did you go for some other reason?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went because I could not stay in Mostar with my children as a result of shelling. We did not have any food. There was nothing to eat there.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Split?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came back from Split at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Madam, at one point you've told us that Mr. Mladen Misic was the be-all and end-all in the territory of Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you -- could we please look at the document number P 02685. That's a document that was shown to you by the Prosecutor. This is a request or a demand by Miljenko Lasic for the appointment of certain people in certain positions but also for Mr. Mladen Misic to be resolved of his duties. You identified this person Misic for us based on this document, and you've told us that this is the same Mr. Misic who was be-all and end-all in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge as to what the reasons for his relief would be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about Mladen Misic having been discharged from his position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that before I saw this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have any more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question, the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your statement, Witness CT, you said that there were people with all sorts of weapons amongst the HVO. Now, my question is: This shooting, was it within a military operation which took place on the 9th of May, 1993, or were these shots deliberately targeting people, people in your home, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 9th of May to expel the Bosniaks from their homes, that was the intention. And our house was particularly targeted because they shouted out the name of my husband and said, "Catch him." They used Zolja-type weapons, pistols, rifles, I don't know what else. But the Zoljas, the hand-held rocket launcher, hit somebody although not the children, luckily, because they'd already gone down to the cellar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two brief questions. In your statement you said you were given dog food in Heliodrom. How did you know? Did you see packages with the label?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband brought those cans from Heliodrom and believe me this was dog food. I've had dogs for years and I know the smell and even my dogs would not eat from those cans. I know what dog food smells like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one more question: You say -- or you've said that the Red Cross had been refused access. They wanted to visit you and were refused. How do you know this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS CS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because UNPROFOR soldiers came. They entered the room where we were, and it looked like a proper prison, and we had two children with us. Their mother was an English teacher, and the children could speak English really well. And in a conversation with these soldiers they learned that they were not allowed to enter. The Red Cross was not allowed to enter to register us women and children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, very quickly, please. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Madam, on the can was there a sign of a dog or a cat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there was. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] The entire food came from the humanitarian aid. It was not produced anywhere in our midst. I'm just checking whether there was a sign on the can.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I saw a dog's head, and I'd know what -- I did it -- I ate -- or, rather, I didn't eat at the Heliodrom. I know very well. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecution don't have any additional questions. Madam, we would like to thank you on behalf of the Judges for having come to The Hague in order to testify and for having provided your statement in writing. I have to call this session to an end because there is another session that follows in a short time. I would like to thank you once again and express my best wishes for your return to your country. I believe that Mr. Mundis is on his feet to tell us something about Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, we're all set pursuant to the court calendar that's been distributed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I invite all of you to come back on Monday at quarter past 2.00 thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 15th day of January, 2007, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.47 p.m.,
